title: A Republic Built on War
question: How did a city that threw out its kings come to rule the Mediterranean?
hook: Rome threw out its kings and then spent the Republic in near-perpetual war.
idea: Republican Rome, an elective oligarchy in near-perpetual war, grew from its surroundings to rule the Mediterranean, until civil wars led by powerful generals broke it.

beats.prompt: In 477 BC the Etruscan city of Veii defeats Rome at the Battle of the Cremera. Eighty years on, in 396 BC, Rome faces Veii again. What happens?

choices.label: Rome loses again and gives up on its Etruscan neighbours
choices.feedback: A second defeat seems likely after the first, but Rome went on to conquer its Etruscan neighbours.

choices.label: The two cities settle into a long truce
choices.feedback: A truce is tempting, but Rome, expanding by war, did not leave Veii standing.

choices.label: Rome destroys Veii, avenging the earlier defeat

beats.explain: The defeat at the Cremera was later avenged at the Battle of Veii in 396 BC, where Rome destroyed the city.

beats.prompt: Put these events of the Republic in order.
items: Civil war between Caesar and Pompey
beats.explain: The kings fell in 509 BC, the Gauls sacked Rome around 387 BC, Zama came in 202 BC and the civil war began in 49 BC.

beats.prompt: Sort each opponent into the group it belongs to.
beats.explain: Rome's first enemies were its Latin and Etruscan neighbours and the Gauls; after Zama it embarked on a long series of conquests against rulers farther away.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: Rome had collective, annual magistracies overseen by a senate.
Annual elections mean ordinary citizens controlled who held the senior offices.
So the Republic was a true democracy.
beats.explain: A number of powerful families largely monopolised the senior magistracies, so the Republic was an elective oligarchy, not a true democracy.
